title: Outdoor Kitchen Gas & Electrical in Ontario: TSSA, ESA and Who Does What
seoTitle: Outdoor Kitchen Gas & Electrical Ontario: TSSA + ESA
seoDescription: In Ontario, outdoor kitchen gas work requires a TSSA-licensed contractor and electrical needs an ESA permit — here is who handles each regulated trade.
tldr: Building an outdoor kitchen in Ontario involves two separate regulatory regimes: TSSA governs all gas connections and appliances, and ESA oversees all electrical work. Gas lines and appliances must maintain minimum 1-metre clearances from combustibles under the Ontario Building Code; electrical circuits require ESA permits and a sign-off inspection before they can be energised. Knowing which licensed contractor handles each regulated trade — and planning conduit runs before the hardscape base goes in — saves time and avoids costly rework.
intro:
An outdoor kitchen project in Barrie or Simcoe County is not a single-trade job. Once you add a gas grill, side burners, a refrigerator, and lighting to an interlocking patio or composite deck build, you are coordinating three separate regulated disciplines: the hardscape contractor who builds the structure, a TSSA-licensed gasfitter who handles all gas work, and a licensed electrical contractor who pulls the ESA permit for every circuit. Each trade has its own inspections and its own body that signs off before the kitchen is put into service.

Most homeowners are surprised to learn how tightly the sequence of this work is constrained. If the gas conduit and electrical conduit are not roughed in before the countertop substrate and cladding are installed, accessing them later means tearing apart a finished structure. Planning the regulatory work upfront — before a single shovel breaks ground — is the difference between a project that finishes on schedule and one that hits an expensive rework halfway through the build. This guide explains what each regulatory body covers, what licences your contractors must hold, and how the sequence works on an actual project.

sections.heading: What TSSA Covers for Outdoor Kitchen Gas Connections
sections.html:
The Technical Standards and Safety Authority — TSSA — is the provincial body that regulates all fuel-gas work in Ontario. Whether you are running natural gas from the house meter to a built-in grill or connecting a propane regulator to a side burner, any gas fitting on your property falls under TSSA jurisdiction. That includes the supply line from the meter, every branch within the outdoor kitchen structure, flexible connectors to appliances, and the final hook-up to gas manifolds, grills, and wok burners.

The licence class matters. A G2 gasfitter is licensed to work on appliances up to 400,000 BTU/hr input — which covers every residential outdoor cooking appliance sold in Canada today. A G1 gasfitter holds the higher-class licence and can work on any gas system regardless of BTU rating. What you cannot do legally in Ontario is have an unlicensed contractor — including your hardscape builder — run gas pipe or connect an appliance, regardless of how simple the connection looks.

TSSA requires a gas-fitting permit for new outdoor kitchen installations. The permit covers a rough-in inspection — confirming pipe routing, pipe sizing, and a pressure test typically run at 0.5 PSI or greater for residential low-pressure systems — and a final inspection once appliances are connected and before the kitchen is put into service. These requirements apply whether the gas source is natural gas from the utility or propane from an on-site tank. The TSSA-licensed gasfitter pulls the permit; if no permit was issued, the work is not legally inspected and the property owner carries all liability.

One thing we coordinate on every outdoor kitchen project in Barrie and Simcoe County: gas conduit or the gas supply stub-out must be roughed in before the countertop substrate and cladding are installed. Once a Unilock or Permacon stone-clad kitchen island is finished, there is no practical way to route gas pipe without demolishing the structure.

sections.heading: What ESA Covers — Outdoor Electrical Always Requires a Permit
sections.html:
The Electrical Safety Authority — ESA — governs all electrical work in Ontario, including every circuit added to an outdoor kitchen structure: receptacles, dedicated appliance circuits, under-counter lighting, exhaust fan wiring, and refrigerator connections. The ESA's requirement is clear: any electrical installation, alteration, or addition requires a permit, an inspection, and sign-off by an ESA electrical inspector before the circuit is energised. There is no exception for small jobs or outdoor structures.

For outdoor kitchen environments, the Ontario Electrical Safety Code requires ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection on all receptacles within 2.5 metres of a water source — which in practice means every outlet in an outdoor kitchen should be GFCI-protected, given proximity to sinks and prep surfaces. Outlets and light fixtures must be wet-location rated (marked WR or listed for damp or wet locations), and any receptacle in a covered outdoor area still exposed to weather must be installed in a weatherproof in-use cover. Standard indoor devices will fail an ESA inspection when installed outdoors.

Dedicated circuits matter for load management. A refrigerator draws 3–5 amps continuously; a built-in pizza oven can pull 15 amps or more; a warming drawer adds another circuit. Running all appliances off a single shared circuit is a common planning mistake that will fail ESA inspection and create a genuine safety hazard in an outdoor wet environment. A licensed electrical contractor (LEC) will size each circuit to its load and document panel capacity to satisfy the inspector.

If you are planning outdoor kitchen lighting — step lights, under-counter accent strips, overhead pergola lighting — all of it falls under the same ESA permit. As part of our outdoor kitchen planning process, we identify every electrical element that needs to be stubbed out before the hardscape base work begins, so there are no rough-in surprises mid-build.

sections.heading: The 3 Regulated Trades — and How They Fit Into the Build Sequence
sections.html:
On a typical outdoor kitchen build in Barrie or Oro-Medonte, three distinct regulated trades are involved. Understanding which one does what — and in which order — is essential for a project that finishes on time without expensive teardowns.

Trade 1 — The Hardscape Contractor. We build the structural base, frame, and finish of the outdoor kitchen: the compacted aggregate base, concrete block or Unilock and Techo-Bloc modular units, countertop substrate, and cladding stone. We also install the utility sleeves and conduit runs that the gas and electrical contractors will later pull wire and pipe through. Our work must happen first — and it must account for every future penetration — because once the structure is clad, accessing the interior without demolition is extremely difficult. Any dimension or location change after cladding is installed costs far more than sorting it out at the design stage.

Trade 2 — The TSSA-Licensed Gasfitter. The gas fitter works in two stages: rough-in before cladding is applied, and final connection once appliances are set. Rough-in covers the supply line run, branch piping sizing, and a pressure test. Final covers appliance connections, flexible connectors rated for the specific appliance BTU output, and the TSSA inspection call. Using a G1- or G2-licensed gas fitter is an Ontario legal requirement, not a preference. Any contractor who quotes the gas work without confirming their TSSA licence class should not be doing the work.

Trade 3 — The Licensed Electrical Contractor. The LEC pulls the ESA permit, installs all wiring and receptacles, and books the ESA inspection at each stage. For a full breakdown of how the planning phase works across all three trades — from design to permit to site sign-off — the planning section of our resource library covers the complete sequence.

sections.heading: Ontario Building Code Clearances for Outdoor Gas Appliances
sections.html:
The Ontario Building Code and manufacturer installation manuals impose specific clearances on outdoor gas appliances that directly influence how an outdoor kitchen layout works. Getting these dimensions into the design before the structure is built prevents costly revisions after the fact.

The most commonly referenced minimum is a 1-metre horizontal clearance from any combustible surface — including wood pergola framing, TimberTech composite decking boards, and vinyl siding on the adjacent house wall — for gas cooking appliances. That 1-metre rule applies to the cooking surface of a built-in grill; side clearances to adjacent countertops (typically natural stone or porcelain, both non-combustible) are governed by the appliance's installation manual, which can specify tighter or wider clearances depending on the model and BTU rating.

Overhead clearance is equally important. The hood or pergola ceiling above an outdoor grill must maintain the minimum clearance listed in the grill's installation manual — typically 900 mm or more above the cooking grate. A wood-lattice pergola at a standard height of 2.1 metres satisfies this clearance for most residential grills, but outdoor kitchen structures with solid roofs require careful measurement. Installing a grill under a low soffit without verifying the clearance is both a fire risk and a permit failure point.

Property line setbacks vary by municipality. In Barrie, the City's zoning bylaw governs how close an outdoor structure can be to a rear or side property line; Innisfil, Oro-Medonte, and Springwater Township each have their own rules. An outdoor kitchen attached to a deck or patio structure may trigger a municipal building permit even if the gas and electrical connections are separately permitted under TSSA and ESA — this is a question for your local building department, and one we flag early in the outdoor kitchen planning process to avoid surprises.

sections.heading: How to Sequence the Regulated Work — Before the Base Goes In
sections.html:
The most expensive mistake on an outdoor kitchen project is starting the hardscape base without a confirmed plan for gas and electrical routing. The sequence below is how we approach a build in Simcoe County.

Before excavation begins: We confirm the gas supply route from the meter or propane tank, the path from the house panel to the outdoor sub-panel or circuit run, and the number and location of every appliance, outlet, and light fixture. This conversation happens with the homeowner and both regulated contractors before any excavation. The gas fitter and electrician need to walk the site and lock in their routes; surprises after the base is poured mean extra cost for everyone on the project.

During base construction: We install conduit sleeves — typically 50–75 mm diameter PVC conduit — through the base structure at every planned penetration point, capped and clearly marked. For gas, we may install the actual supply line before the surface stone goes down if the gas fitter is available at that stage; otherwise, we pull a draw string through the conduit so the fitter can later pull CSST flexible gas piping or hard pipe through without opening the structure. For electrical, we leave a minimum 100 mm of conduit stub protruding above the base at each outlet or switch location.

After the structure is clad: The gas fitter connects all appliances, performs the pressure test, and calls TSSA for inspection. The electrician makes final connections, installs devices and covers, and calls ESA for inspection. The kitchen cannot legally be put into service until both inspections are signed off. Any use of the gas connections before TSSA sign-off is a liability and safety issue that no reputable contractor will permit.

If you want a site-specific sequencing plan for your project in Barrie or across Simcoe County, contact us to book a site visit and we will walk through routing, appliance layout, and the coordination of all three trades. You can also use our online cost estimator to get a planning-level figure on the hardscape portion before we meet.

faqs.question: Do I need a permit to build an outdoor kitchen in Ontario?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases — at minimum two separate permits. Any gas work requires a gas-fitting permit issued under TSSA authority; any electrical work requires an electrical permit from ESA. Whether the structure itself requires a municipal building permit depends on your municipality and the nature of the build. In Barrie, a freestanding outdoor kitchen island or one attached to an existing deck may trigger a building permit review; the City's building department can confirm. Oro-Medonte and Springwater Township have their own rules. The practical rule of thumb is to assume at least 2 regulated permits and to check with your municipality about a possible third before construction starts.

faqs.question: Can my landscaping contractor run the outdoor kitchen gas line?
faqs.answer: No. In Ontario, any gas fitting — installing gas pipe, connecting an appliance, or modifying an existing line — must be performed by a TSSA-licensed gasfitter holding a G1 or G2 licence. A hardscape or landscaping contractor can install conduit sleeves and coordinate sequencing, but cannot legally touch the gas pipe or make any gas connection, regardless of their experience level. This rule exists for safety reasons, and unlicensed gas work can create liability exposure and insurance complications for the property owner.

faqs.question: What clearance does an outdoor grill need from combustible surfaces in Ontario?
faqs.answer: The Ontario Building Code requires a minimum 1-metre horizontal clearance from any combustible material — including wood framing, composite decking, and siding — for gas cooking appliances. Individual appliance installation manuals may specify additional clearances that take precedence over the code minimum if they are more restrictive. Always verify the installation manual for your specific appliance model; clearance requirements vary by brand and BTU rating. Your TSSA-licensed gasfitter confirms compliance as part of the rough-in inspection before cladding is installed.

faqs.question: Does an outdoor kitchen need GFCI-protected outlets?
faqs.answer: Yes. The Ontario Electrical Safety Code requires GFCI protection on outdoor receptacles and on any receptacle located within 2.5 metres of a water source — both conditions apply to a typical outdoor kitchen. In practice, every outlet in an outdoor kitchen should be GFCI-protected, installed in a weatherproof in-use cover, and rated for wet or damp locations. Standard indoor devices do not meet the Electrical Code standard for outdoor kitchen installations and will fail an ESA inspection.

faqs.question: How far in advance should I book a TSSA gasfitter and an ESA electrician?
faqs.answer: For projects in Simcoe County, planning these trades 4–8 weeks ahead of your construction start is a reasonable buffer. Licensed gas fitters and electrical contractors in the Barrie area book quickly during the May-to-September outdoor-project season. Securing your gas fitter and electrician before the hardscape work begins — not during or after — is how projects stay on schedule. ESA and TSSA inspection timelines depend on the local office's availability at the time of the inspection request, which your licensed contractor will manage.

faqs.question: Can I use propane instead of natural gas to avoid the gas line installation?
faqs.answer: Using propane does not eliminate TSSA-regulated work; it changes the scope. A propane outdoor kitchen requires a properly sized regulator, code-compliant tank placement (the Technical Standards and Safety Act sets minimum distances from windows, doors, and ignition sources), and TSSA-licensed connection of all appliances and piping. For rural Simcoe County properties in Innisfil or Oro-Medonte that do not have natural gas service, propane is often the practical choice — but the regulatory requirements for propane are parallel to natural gas, not simpler.

faqs.question: Will my outdoor kitchen project involve three separate contractors at once?
faqs.answer: Not simultaneously, but yes — three regulated trades are typically involved at different stages. The hardscape contractor builds the base, structure, and cladding; the TSSA-licensed gas fitter handles gas rough-in and final appliance connection; the licensed electrical contractor runs wiring and books the ESA inspection. The hardscape contractor works first; gas and electrical rough-in follows during or immediately after structural framing; final connections are made after cladding is complete. The key is pre-planning the full sequence before work begins, which is why we include the gas fitter and electrician in the site consultation from the outset.
